briefing: It is a Monday morning at Market Row Community Credit Union. J. Smith, a member services representative, tells the help desk that something is off: there has been no sign-in from them yet today, but their account looks busy.

You are the analyst on call. Everything on screen is synthetic training data, but treat it the way you would treat the real thing: look at what the logs actually say, collect evidence, and only claim what the evidence can support.
Your job is not to guess who did this. It is to work out what happened, which systems are affected, and what a proportionate next step looks like.

objectives.text: Find the key sign-in, MFA and portal events for the reported account.
Build an accurate timeline from evidence you collected.
Keep confirmed facts separate from hypotheses and open questions.
Name the affected systems and set a proportionate severity.
Recommend a response that fits the evidence.
Write a clear summary and escalate to the right person.

community_impact: Market Row members trust the credit union with their savings, loans and contact details. If a staff account is taken over, the member support portal could expose those details. A calm, well-documented response protects members and keeps the branch open for the neighbours who rely on it.

learning_objectives.title: Authentication
learning_objectives.explanation: Authentication is how a system checks that you are who you say you are. A sign-in event records who tried, from where, on what device and whether it worked.

learning_objectives.title: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
learning_objectives.explanation: MFA asks for a second proof, such as a code or approval on a phone you already enrolled. Adding a new MFA device is a sensitive change, because whoever controls that device can pass the second check.

learning_objectives.title: Suspicious login patterns
learning_objectives.explanation: Repeated failures followed by a success, a sign-in from a source the person never uses, or activity when they say they were not working are all patterns worth a closer look. A pattern is a lead, not a verdict.

learning_objectives.title: SIEM filtering
learning_objectives.explanation: A SIEM collects logs from many places into one searchable view. Filtering by account, source, result and time turns thousands of events into the few that matter.

learning_objectives.title: Evidence handling
learning_objectives.explanation: Evidence is the specific log events behind a claim. Collect it with its event IDs so anyone can check your work, and do not alter the original records.

learning_objectives.title: Timeline reconstruction
learning_objectives.explanation: Putting evidence in time order shows cause and effect: what happened first, what followed, and how long each step took.

learning_objectives.title: Incident response
learning_objectives.explanation: Response is a sequence: verify, scope, contain, preserve, recover. Match the action to the evidence. Shutting everything down is rarely proportionate.

learning_objectives.title: Documentation
learning_objectives.explanation: A good case file states facts with evidence, labels guesses as hypotheses, lists what is still unknown, and ends with a clear recommendation another analyst can act on.

knowledge_checks.question: An account shows two failed sign-ins and then a success from a source it has never used. What is the best description?

options.text: Proof that the account was hacked.
options.feedback: Not yet. The pattern is worth investigating, but a pattern alone is a lead. Look for corroborating evidence before you call it proof.

options.text: A pattern worth investigating that needs more evidence.
options.feedback: Right. It is an indicator, not a conclusion. Next you would check the source, the device and what happened after the sign-in.

options.text: Normal behaviour, so it can be ignored.
options.feedback: A new source plus earlier failures is not what this person normally does. Ignoring it would skip a real lead.

knowledge_checks.question: Why does a new MFA device enrollment right after a suspicious sign-in matter?

options.text: It means the sign-in was safe.
options.feedback: The opposite can be true: enrolling a device can give someone lasting access.

options.text: It could let whoever controls that device pass the second check later.
options.feedback: Yes. That is why an unexpected enrollment is treated as a high-value event and goes into the evidence.
They are logged, and the log is exactly where you find them.

knowledge_checks.question: You believe the employee's password was guessed, but no event shows how. How should you record it?

options.text: As a fact, so the report sounds confident.
options.feedback: A fact needs evidence behind it. Writing a guess as a fact is the kind of error a reviewer will flag.

options.text: As a hypothesis, and list what would confirm it.
options.feedback: Good. Hypotheses and unknowns keep the case honest and tell the next analyst where to look.

options.text: Leave it out of the case file.
options.feedback: Leaving out an open question hides a gap. Record it as an unknown or a hypothesis.

knowledge_checks.question: One employee account looks affected. Which first response is the most proportionate?

options.text: Shut down all staff sign-ins and member services.
options.feedback: That harms every member and every colleague to address one account.

options.text: Verify with the employee on a known number, then protect the account.
options.feedback: Yes. Verify first, then reset the password, end sessions and review the MFA change.
Waiting leaves a possibly compromised account active while member data is within reach.

career_preview.title: Foundations
career_preview.note: Reading logs, collecting evidence and writing an honest case file.

career_preview.title: Endpoint and identity defense

career_preview.title: Incident coordination
career_preview.note: Leading a response with other teams while keeping the record clear.
